Naked but for goatskin belts, the Luperci run round the Palatine striking women with thongs of goat hide to make them fertile
In the Forum: in 44 BC Antony, running as a Lupercus, offered Caesar a diadem at the Rostra
Return to the Lupercal

Esquilina region: shrines on the Oppius, Fagutal and Cispius
Collina region: shrines on the Quirinal and Viminal

routes.n: Ludi Saeculares of 17 BC

stops.t: Nights of 31 May-2 June: Augustus sacrifices at the Tarentum by the Tiber to the Moirai, the Ilithyiae and Terra Mater; Agrippa joins him
Days 1 and 2: white bulls to Jupiter and a white cow to Juno on the Capitol; 110 matrons hold sellisternia
Day 3: sacrifice to Apollo and Diana at the Palatine temple; 27 boys and 27 girls sing Horace's Carmen Saeculare
The hymn is sung again on the Capitol

routes.n: Entry of Constantine (29 October 312)

stops.t: After the battle of 28 October Maxentius' body is pulled from the Tiber by the Milvian Bridge; his head is carried on a spear before the army
Through the Porta Flaminia; the Senate and people pour out to meet the victor
Down the Via Lata towards the Forum
The Forum and Senate house: Constantine promises to restore the Senate's dignity
He goes up to the Palatine palace; the panegyrist of 313 notes he did not climb the Capitol to sacrifice

routes.n: Visit of Theodoric to Rome (500)

stops.t: Pope Symmachus, the Senate and people meet the Arian king outside the city; he prays at St Peter's 'as devoutly as a Catholic'
Enters the city across the Tiber
Visits the Senate in the Curia
Addresses the people at the place called 'ad Palmam' in the Forum, promising to keep the laws of the emperors

Takes up residence in the Palatine palace; holds his tricennalia, gives circus games and grants 120,000 modii of grain a year to the poor and 200 pounds of gold a year for repairing the palace and walls

routes.n: Totila takes Rome (17 December 546)

stops.t: Four Isaurian guards let the Goths in through the Porta Asinaria at night
Through the deserted city: most of the starving population had already fled with Bessas' garrison
Totila goes to pray at St Peter's, where the deacon Pelagius begs him to spare the people; he threatens to raze Rome and turn it into pasture, and pulls down parts of the walls

routes.n: Funeral procession of Julius Caesar (March 44 BC)

stops.t: The body is carried by magistrates from the Domus Publica, his official house as pontifex maximus
Laid in a gilded shrine modelled on the Temple of Venus Genetrix before the Rostra; Antony's eulogy and the display of the bloodied toga and a wax effigy with the 23 wounds inflame the crowd
Instead of taking the bier to the pyre prepared in the Campus Martius by Julia's tomb, the crowd burns it in the Forum on benches and furniture; the Temple of Divus Iulius later rises on the spot

stops.t: From the family house on the Palatine slope, preceded by musicians and mourners, actors wear the wax masks of the ancestors in the robes of their highest office
At the Rostra the 'ancestors' sit on ivory chairs while a son delivers the eulogy of the dead man and of each ancestor in turn
Out through the Porta Capena
Burial or cremation at the family tomb on the Via Appia, as at the Tomb of the Scipios

routes.n: Flight and death of Gaius Gracchus (121 BC)

stops.t: Gracchus and Fulvius Flaccus hold the Aventine with their armed supporters; Gracchus withdraws to the Temple of Diana and is stopped by friends from killing himself
Down past the Porta Trigemina to the river as the consul Opimius' men with Cretan archers storm the hill
At the Pons Sublicius his friends Pomponius and Laetorius hold off the pursuers and are killed
In the grove of Furrina on the Janiculum his slave Philocrates kills him and then himself; his head is taken to Opimius for its weight in gold. About 3,000 of his followers are killed

routes.n: Gallic advance into Rome (390 BC)

stops.t: Three days after the rout at the Allia the Gauls under Brennus come down the Via Salaria
They find the Porta Collina open and the city undefended
In the Forum the old senators sit in their doorways in their robes of office; M. Papirius strikes a Gaul who strokes his beard and the massacre begins. The city is burned
A night attempt to climb the Capitol near the shrine of Carmenta is foiled when Juno's geese wake M. Manlius
After a seven-month siege the Capitol's defenders pay a ransom of 1,000 pounds of gold

routes.n: Alaric's Goths enter Rome (24 August 410)

stops.t: At night the gate of the Via Salaria is opened (by treachery or by the slaves of a noblewoman, according to rival stories)
The Goths burn the houses by the gate, including the old palace in the Gardens of Sallust
The Basilica Aemilia burns; bronze coins melted into its floor are still visible; the Secretarium Senatus is damaged
On the Aventine the rich houses are plundered; Marcella is beaten
The Goths respect the basilicas of Peter and Paul as asylum; sacred vessels are carried there in procession under guard

tours.title: The city of the first consuls

stops.title: The new temple on the Capitol
stops.text: Tradition dates the dedication of the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus to 509 BC, the first year of the Republic. Its podium, about 53 by 62 m, was one of the largest in the Mediterranean, built for an Etruscan-style temple with three cellae for Jupiter, Juno and Minerva.

stops.title: The Forum valley
stops.text: Below the Capitol the valley had been drained and filled in the late 7th century, with the stream canalised into what became the Cloaca Maxima. The Forum was a trodden earth and gravel square ringed by shops, shrines and the Regia.

stops.title: Comitium and Curia
stops.text: The assembly place of the Comitium and the senate house traditionally ascribed to Tullus Hostilius stood at the north-west corner of the square, by the black stone of the Lapis Niger and its archaic inscription.

stops.title: The Palatine
stops.text: Iron Age huts had stood on the Germalus since the 9th and 8th centuries BC. The hut the Romans called the house of Romulus was kept and repaired for centuries as a relic.

stops.title: Forum Boarium and the river harbour
stops.text: By the Tiber crossing, the cattle market and the river port drew traders from Etruria, Latium and the Greek world. The twin temples under Sant'Omobono, for Fortuna and Mater Matuta, belong to this archaic waterfront.

stops.title: The early city as a whole
stops.text: Rome around 500 BC was a large city by Italian standards, its houses clustered on the hills around the Forum valley. The stone circuit later credited to Servius Tullius dates mostly from after the Gallic sack of 390 BC.

stops.title: The Domus Publica
stops.text: As pontifex maximus Caesar lived in the official house by the Atrium Vestae on the Sacra Via. On the morning of 15 March, after Calpurnia's dreams and bad omens, he set out late for the senate.

stops.title: The Curia of Pompey
stops.text: The senate met in the hall at the east end of the Porticus of Pompey, now under Largo di Torre Argentina, because the Curia in the Forum was being rebuilt. Caesar was stabbed twenty-three times and fell at the base of Pompey's statue.

stops.title: Pompey's theatre
stops.text: The first permanent stone theatre in Rome (55 BC), with the Temple of Venus Victrix at the top of its cavea and a great garden portico behind the stage. The conspirators had gathered here in the morning.

stops.title: Caesar's unfinished forum
stops.text: Dedicated in 46 BC though not complete, the Forum of Caesar with its Temple of Venus Genetrix was the first of the imperial fora, laid out on land bought for tens of millions of sesterces.

stops.title: The Rostra and the funeral
stops.text: At Caesar's funeral on about 20 March, Antony spoke from the Rostra and displayed the bloodied toga. The crowd built a pyre on the spot and burned the body in the Forum itself.

stops.title: The Temple of Divus Julius
stops.text: Where the body burned, Octavian dedicated the Temple of the Deified Julius in 29 BC, its podium faced with the beaks of ships taken at Actium. The ruined altar in front still marks the pyre site.

stops.title: The Forum of Augustus
stops.text: Vowed at Philippi and dedicated in 2 BC, the forum and its Temple of Mars Ultor sat behind a fire wall of peperino over 30 m high that shut out the Subura.

stops.title: The Palatine house and Apollo
stops.text: Augustus lived in a modest house on the Palatine, next to the Temple of Apollo (28 BC) with its porticoes and Greek and Latin libraries.

stops.title: The Theatre of Marcellus
stops.text: Begun by Caesar and dedicated in 13 or 11 BC in memory of Augustus' nephew and heir, it seated perhaps 11,000 to 15,000 behind three storeys of travertine arcades.

stops.title: Agrippa's Campus Martius
stops.text: Agrippa transformed the Campus: the first Pantheon (finished 25 BC), the Baths of Agrippa fed by the Aqua Virgo, the Saepta Julia voting hall and the Stagnum lake.

stops.title: The Ara Pacis
stops.text: The Altar of Augustan Peace, dedicated in 9 BC beside the Via Flaminia, stood in a marble enclosure carved with the imperial family in procession.

stops.title: The Mausoleum
stops.text: Augustus died on 19 August AD 14 at Nola. His ashes were placed in the great drum tomb he had built in 28 BC, 87 m across and planted with trees.

stops.title: Where it started
stops.text: On the night of 18 to 19 July 64 fire broke out in shops full of flammable goods at the end of the Circus Maximus near the Palatine and Caelian (Tacitus, Annals 15.38).

stops.title: Through the valley and up the hills
stops.text: Driven by wind it raced along the Circus and up the slopes. It burned for six days before being halted at the foot of the Esquiline by demolitions, then flared again from the property of Tigellinus.

stops.title: Three regions destroyed
stops.text: Of the fourteen regions, three were levelled and seven badly damaged. Among the losses were ancient temples, Nero's own Domus Transitoria, and houses of the old Republican nobility.

stops.title: The Golden House
stops.text: Nero used the burned land for the Domus Aurea, a palace landscape with a lake in the valley where the Colosseum would rise, and a colossal bronze statue of himself in the vestibule.

stops.title: The Flavian answer
stops.text: Vespasian drained Nero's lake and gave the site back to the people: the Flavian Amphitheatre, dedicated by Titus in 80 with a hundred days of games.

stops.title: The Pantheon
stops.text: Rebuilt under Hadrian (about 113 to 125) with Agrippa's name restored on the pediment. The unreinforced concrete dome spans 43.3 m, still the largest of its kind.

stops.title: The Temple of Venus and Roma
stops.text: Hadrian's own design on the Velia, dedicated about 135: two cellae back to back on a platform about 145 by 100 m. Apollodorus reportedly criticised it.

stops.title: Trajan's Forum
stops.text: The largest of the imperial fora, finished in 112 and 113: the Basilica Ulpia, the libraries and the column whose spiral relief narrates the Dacian wars.

stops.title: The Mausoleum of Hadrian
stops.text: Built across the Tiber with its own bridge, the Pons Aelius, and finished in 139 after Hadrian's death. It later became the Castel Sant'Angelo.

stops.title: The city at its height
stops.text: Under the Antonines Rome held perhaps a million people. Eleven aqueducts brought water, and apartment blocks rose to the legal limit of about 60 feet set by Trajan.

stops.title: The basilica Maxentius began
stops.text: Maxentius began the great vaulted basilica on the Velia. Constantine finished it after defeating him at the Milvian Bridge on 28 October 312, reorienting it with a new entrance on the Sacra Via.

stops.title: The Arch of Constantine
stops.text: Dedicated in 315 for his tenth anniversary, the arch reused reliefs from monuments of Trajan, Hadrian and Marcus Aurelius beside new Constantinian friezes.

stops.title: The Lateran
stops.text: On the site of the demolished barracks of the horse guards who fought for Maxentius, Constantine built the cathedral of Rome, the Basilica Salvatoris, from about 312.

stops.title: St Peter's on the Vatican
stops.text: A five-aisled basilica was cut into the Vatican hillside over the shrine believed to mark Peter's grave, levelling a cemetery to build it.

stops.title: Baths of Diocletian
stops.text: Finished about 306, the largest baths in Rome covered some 13 hectares. They kept working into the 6th century, until the Goths cut the aqueducts in 537.

stops.title: The Porta Salaria, 24 August 410
stops.text: Alaric's Goths entered by the Salarian Gate at night. For three days they plundered the city, the first time Rome had fallen to an enemy since the Gauls almost 800 years earlier.

stops.title: The Gardens of Sallust
stops.text: The palace in the Horti Sallustiani near the gate was burned, according to Procopius, and was never restored.

stops.title: The Basilica Aemilia
stops.text: Fire swept the Basilica Aemilia. Bronze coins of the money-changers melted into its floor, where excavators found them still fused to the marble.

stops.title: Hadrian's Mausoleum under siege
stops.text: In 537 Vitiges' Goths besieged Belisarius. At the mausoleum, now part of the defences, the defenders broke up the statues and threw them down on the attackers (Procopius, Wars 5.22).

stops.title: The Porta Asinaria, 546
stops.text: Totila took the city when Isaurian guards opened the Asinarian Gate. Procopius says the population was carried off and the city left empty for a time.

stops.title: The Pantheon becomes a church
stops.text: With permission from the emperor Phocas, Pope Boniface IV consecrated the Pantheon as Santa Maria ad Martyres in 609, a year after Phocas' column rose in the Forum.

population: End of the monarchy. The archaic city of about 285 ha (Ampolo, Cornell) may have held 20,000-40,000; Plutarch's census of 130,000 for 508 BC (Publicola 12) counts the whole citizen body of the territory and is doubtful.
Gallic sack; afterwards the 11 km Servian Wall (from 378 BC) encloses 426 ha, far more than was built up.
Aqua Appia, the first aqueduct, and the Via Appia: the city outgrows its springs.
Start of the First Punic War; Rome the largest city of Italy after Tarentum and Capua.
After the Second Punic War, refugees and freed slaves swell the plebs.
Age of the Gracchi: land crisis drives migration to the city; Gaius Gracchus' grain law of 123.
Lex Terentia Cassia (73) restores grain sales; perhaps 40,000 recipients rising fast.
Clodius makes the grain ration free (58); recipients soar to 320,000 adult male citizens by 46.
Caesar's revision of the lists cuts recipients from 320,000 to 150,000 (Suetonius Iul. 41.3), partly by settling 80,000 colonists overseas.

Augustus pays 60 denarii each to 320,000 of the urban plebs in 5 BC (Res Gestae 15) and limits grain recipients to about 200,000 in 2 BC (Dio 55.10.1). Adding women, children, slaves, soldiers and foreigners gives the 'Great Rome' figure of about 1 million (Lo Cascio, Morley, Hopkins); Storey's density method gives about 450,000.
Death of Augustus. Strabo describes continuous building and the 70-foot height limit.
Great Fire: of 14 regions, 3 destroyed and 7 badly damaged (Tacitus Ann. 15.40).
Trajanic peak of public building; Trajan lowers the height limit to 60 feet.
Antonine plague arrives with the army returning from the East; mortality in the city perhaps 10-20 per cent over the following decades.
Severan Rome; the plebs frumentaria perhaps 150,000-200,000 men; the Marble Plan maps the city.
The Aurelian Wall (19 km) encloses 1,372 ha; Aurelian replaces grain with free bread and adds pork, oil and cheap wine.
Constantine. The Regionary Catalogues of the mid-4th century count 46,602 insulae and 1,790 domus, 290 horrea, 254 bakeries.
Constantius II's visit (Ammianus 16.10) finds a city of overwhelming monuments.
Krautheimer's figure of about 800,000 is a high estimate; many now prefer 500,000 or less for the late 4th century.
Alaric's first siege brings famine and plague (Zosimus 5.39).
Pork distribution data (Nov. Val. 36) have been used to estimate 120,000-200,000 recipients and a population of perhaps 400,000-500,000 in the early 5th century.
Valentinian III lowers the pork contributions owing to fewer consumers; the fall since 410 is clear but its size disputed.
Vandal sack (14 days of plunder); captives carried to Carthage.
Theodoric's visit; restorations by the Ostrogothic kings. Cassiodorus still speaks of a large populace living on the old supply system.
Gothic siege of 537-538: aqueducts cut, the hills lose their water and their people.
Totila takes the city; Procopius (Wars 7.22.19) claims it was left with no inhabitants at all for 40 days, a rhetorical exaggeration.
End of the Gothic War: the population, concentrated in the Campus Martius and Trastevere, is put at about 30,000 by Krautheimer.
Plague and flood; Gregory organises food relief through the church's estates and diaconiae.
Early medieval city of perhaps 30,000-60,000 inside a wall built for ten times as many.
